methodological_rigor.justification: This is a retrospective dosimetric comparison of 34 pediatric multi-isocenter VMAT-TBI cases (21 FBCT-guided vs 13 CBCT-guided), with inclusion/exclusion criteria stated and baseline characteristics reported as balanced (Table 1). The planning approach was standardized across centers (same planning/review team and explicit plan acceptance criteria), which supports internal consistency, but the study evaluates recalculated dose metrics rather than clinical outcomes and acknowledges limited sample size and omission of dynamic factors like respiratory motion. Statistical comparisons report multiple dosimetric endpoints with P-values (e.g., V90%, V100%, V110%, HI/CI, lung/kidney mean dose), but the manuscript does not clearly specify the statistical tests, does not report confidence intervals for group differences, and does not discuss multiplicity despite many correlated comparisons.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is a retrospective, two-center comparative analysis of treated pediatric TBI patients focused on dosimetric endpoints, which fits Oxford LoE 4 (case-series/retrospective comparative cohort without prospective control). Clinically, the question is directly relevant to pediatric TBI delivery because small setup errors at multi-isocenter junctions can cause under- or overdosing, and the study reports improved PTV coverage/homogeneity and slightly lower mean lung/kidney doses with integrated FBCT guidance (e.g., 12 Gy regimen V100% 92.81% vs 90.40% and mean lung dose 8.47 vs 8.61 Gy). While the absolute organ-dose differences are modest, workflow implications (single whole-body scan and one couch correction) could meaningfully affect safety and feasibility in children.

reporting_quality.justification: As a retrospective observational comparison of two clinical workflows, STROBE is the closest applicable standard; the manuscript describes eligibility criteria, imaging workflows at each center, predefined dosimetric metrics, and provides baseline comparability and tabulated results. However, key reporting details are thin: statistical methods are not fully specified, there is no clear patient-flow diagram beyond textual inclusion/exclusion, and the analysis is limited to dosimetry without prespecified clinical endpoints or protocol registration. No code or dataset deposit is described in the normalized text, and underlying planning/IGRT dose data appear unavailable, so reproducibility relies mainly on narrative workflow description rather than shared materials.

novelty_literature.justification: The manuscript’s main novel element is a head-to-head, real-world comparison of integrated long-length FBCT-based multi-isocenter alignment versus sequential per-isocenter CBCT localization for pediatric multi-isocenter TBI, evaluated across both 12 Gy/6F and 3 Gy/1F regimens. The contribution is largely incremental (workflow/QA optimization) rather than a new biological or therapeutic concept, and the reported improvements are in dosimetric surrogates (coverage/homogeneity and small mean lung/kidney dose reductions). The paper positions itself against prior TBI technique and setup-error literature, but the novelty is mainly in directly contrasting these two IGRT calibration strategies in children.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally clear and logically organized, with a concrete abstract that reports sample sizes, regimens, and key dose metrics (e.g., V90/V100/V110, HI/CI, organ mean doses). Methods describe the two IGRT workflows step-by-step and define the dosimetric endpoints and plan acceptance criteria, and figure/table captions are informative given the blinded format. Some passages are wordy and a few definitions are awkwardly inserted (e.g., PTV definition text), but overall readability is good and the discussion connects observed differences to junction error mechanisms.

key_strengths: Direct comparison of integrated FBCT versus sequential CBCT alignment for pediatric multi-isocenter VMAT-TBI using real treated patients and two dose regimens (12 Gy/6F and 3 Gy/1F).
Standardized planning and QC across centers (same physics/oncology team and explicit plan acceptance criteria), reducing protocol heterogeneity.
Consistent direction of effect across multiple PTV coverage/homogeneity metrics (higher V90/V100, lower V110, improved HI/CI) and modest reductions in mean lung and kidney doses.
key_concerns: Retrospective design with small sample size (34 total; 21 vs 13) and reliance on dosimetric surrogates without clinical toxicity or outcome validation.
Statistical reporting is incomplete (tests not clearly specified, no effect-size confidence intervals, and no discussion of multiplicity across many correlated endpoints).
Generalizability is limited by equipment availability (FBCT-linac) and the absence of assessment of motion/deformation effects (e.g., respiratory motion) on junction dosimetry.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The study is a solid, clinically relevant workflow/dosimetry comparison but is constrained by retrospective design, small N, and limited statistical/reporting depth; it fits as a tier-3 technical/clinical methods contribution pending clearer analytic reporting and stronger validation.
